Q235.L1t: Pew Research surveys have long compared how religious belief is linked to views about morality across many countries.
Q235.L2t: The 2019 Pew survey asked people in many countries whether belief in God is necessary for being moral, and answers varied widely by country.
Q235.L3t: In the 2019 Pew survey, South Korea fell between the very secular, low-percentage Western European countries and the high-percentage countries of Africa and South Asia, with a figure clearly above one in four but below a majority.
Q235.L4t: Roughly four in ten South Koreans, a bit under half, said belief in God is necessary for morality.
Q235.L2f: The Pew survey on belief in God and morality was conducted only in Asian countries, and South Korea was the first country surveyed.
Q235.L3f: South Koreans are among the most secular people in the world, so only a small minority, about one in four, link belief in God to morality in the 2019 survey.
Q235.L4f: About a quarter of South Koreans said belief in God is necessary to be moral, so the lowest figure is the right one.

Q212.L1t: Bullying among adolescents has been measured by international organizations using school-based surveys in many countries.
Q212.L2t: Data on bullying of 13-15 year olds in Japan come from a 2015 international school survey asking about incidents in the previous couple of months.
Q212.L3t: The 2015 figure for Japan was well above the single-digit and low-teens rates but far below a majority, at a little over one in three students.
Q212.L4t: About thirty-six percent of Japanese children aged 13-15 said they had been bullied at least once in the past couple of months.
Q212.L2f: The 2015 Japan bullying data came from a survey of university students and asked only about bullying over the previous decade.
Q212.L3f: In Japan the 2015 survey showed a majority of students, around two in three, had been bullied recently, reflecting very high school bullying rates.
Q212.L4f: About two-thirds of Japanese children aged 13-15 reported being bullied at least once in the past couple of months, so the highest figure is right.

Q261.L1t: Life expectancy differs substantially across countries, shaped by income, health care, and public health conditions.
Q261.L2t: Life expectancy figures for 2019 for these four countries all fall between roughly the early 70s and the late 70s years.
Q261.L3t: In 2019 Brazil, China and Iran each had life expectancy a few years above Mexico's, which was held down by high rates of diabetes, obesity and violence-related deaths.
Q261.L4t: Mexico had the lowest life expectancy of the four countries in 2019.
Q261.L2f: In 2019 all four countries listed had life expectancy figures below 65 years because of widespread infectious disease.
Q261.L3f: Brazil's life expectancy in 2019 was a few years below that of Mexico, China and Iran, because of its much weaker health care and higher mortality overall.
Q261.L4f: Brazil had the lowest life expectancy of the four countries in 2019.
